title: John 13:31–38
context: When Judas has gone, Jesus says now the Son of Man is glorified, and God in Him. He will be with them only a little longer; they cannot follow now. A new commandment: love one another as He has loved them; by this all will know they are His disciples. Peter asks why he cannot follow now and vows his life. Jesus answers with the rooster: the denier before dawn.

voices.heading: Voices from both camps
voices.intro: How earlier teachers on both sides handled the new commandment and a disciple’s vowed life, quoted directly.
voices.note: Quotations lightly abridged for length; wording follows standard English translations of the sources named.

arminian.quote: A new commandment I give unto you, that ye love one another; as I have loved you. By this shall all men know that ye are my disciples. Wilt thou lay down thy life for my sake? The cock shall not crow, till thou hast denied me thrice.
arminian.source: Explanatory Notes upon the New Testament (on John 13:34–38)

reformed.quote: The commandment is called new, because he sets before them his own example. By this love they will be known as his. Peter’s rash confidence is reproved: he will deny him thrice before the cock crows.

verses.text: When he had gone out, Jesus said, “Now the Son of Man has been glorified, and God has been glorified in him.
verses.arminianNotes:
The night of v. 30 is, in His mouth, the now of glory.

Judas’s exit starts the public path to the cross, and Jesus calls that glorifying. Glory is not only later shine; it is obedient love visible.
verses.reformedNotes:
Now: after the traitor’s leaving, glory language.

“Now”—the hour of 12:23 and 13:1 speaks. God glorified in the Son of Man includes this handing-over.

verses.text: If God has been glorified in him, God will also glorify him in himself, and he will glorify him immediately.
verses.arminianNotes:
If / will / at once: the Father’s answering glory is not delayed to a remote age only.

At once includes resurrection and the name above every name, pledged to the One walking toward Friday.
verses.reformedNotes:
God will glorify him in himself, at once.

The Son’s glorifying of God is met by God’s glorifying of the Son. At once is the Father’s speed.

verses.text: Little children, I will be with you a little while longer. You will seek me, and as I said to the Jews, ‘Where I am going, you can’t come,’ so now I tell you.
verses.arminianNotes:
Little children—tender, after glory-talk. A little while; you cannot come where I am going, the same line once said to “the Jews.”

Even His own cannot follow this hour. 14:1–3 will promise a later taking; tonight’s cannot is true.
verses.reformedNotes:
Little children / cannot come. The restriction is for this going.

Later they will follow (v. 36). The cannot is timed to the unique hour of atonement.

verses.text: A new commandment I give to you, that you love one another. Just as I have loved you, you also love one another.
verses.arminianNotes:
New commandment: love one another, even as I have loved you. New because the measure is now His own love, heading to the basin and the cross. Wesley and Calvin both mark the example.

This is command, not mood. As I have loved you is the standard grace enables in a people who must actually love.
verses.reformedNotes:
Calvin: new because He sets His own example. Just as I have loved you.

Leviticus already said love neighbor; the newness is the as of the crucified Lord as the community’s law.
verses.keyContrast: The new command is mutual love measured by Jesus’ love. Arminians stress the enabled duty of the as. Reformed readers stress that His prior love is both pattern and power of theirs.

verses.text: By this everyone will know that you are my disciples, if you have love for one another.”
verses.arminianNotes:
The world’s knowledge of their discipleship hangs on if you have love. Apologetics here is a common life.

All people will know—or not. The if is the church’s visible test, sincerely laid on them.
verses.reformedNotes:
By this all will know / if you have love.

Doctrine without this love fails the Lord’s own ID badge. The if is the appointed evidence, not a rival gospel.

verses.text: Simon Peter said to him, “Lord, where are you going?” Jesus answered, “Where I am going, you can’t follow now, but you will follow afterwards.”
verses.arminianNotes:
Where? Cannot now, will afterward. Peter’s story is already a now and a later (21:19).

The cannot is not a never. Afterward includes restoration after the rooster. Following is still the calling.
verses.reformedNotes:
Cannot now / will afterward: Peter’s two tenses.

The Lord writes Peter’s martyrdom into afterward while forbidding tonight’s heroics.

verses.text: Peter said to him, “Lord, why can’t I follow you now? I will lay down my life for you.”
verses.arminianNotes:
Why not now, plus a vow of his life. The will is loud and sincere and about to fail.

Zeal is distinct from ability. He needs the washing he almost refused and the Spirit not yet given; the vow without that is a trap.
verses.reformedNotes:
Why can I not / I will lay down my life. Rash confidence, Calvin said.

The Shepherd will lay down His life for Peter, not first the other way. The vow inverts the gospel.

verses.text: Jesus answered him, “Will you lay down your life for me? Most certainly I tell you, the rooster won’t crow until you have denied me three times.
verses.arminianNotes:
Will you?—then the rooster and three denials before dawn. Foreknowledge is mercy that will hurt.

A true disciple can deny. The prediction is meant to be remembered when he weeps, so that afterward (v. 36) still stands. Falling is not treated as impossible, nor as the last word.
verses.reformedNotes:
Will you lay down your life for me? The question unmasks the vow.

Reformed mercy in the wound: Jesus knows the denials and still calls him little child, still promises afterward. Peter’s collapse is certain tonight; it is not the end of being His.
